claim: PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2 are directly activated by tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Direct activation of the human phospholipase C-γ isozymes (PLC-γ1, -γ2) by tyrosine phosphorylation is fundamental to the control of diverse biological processes, including chemotaxis, platelet aggregation, and adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a fundamental property of PLC-γ isozymes and is supported by extensive literature citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Aberrant activation of PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2 is implicated in inflammation, autoimmunity, and cancer.
source: In turn, aberrant activation of PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2 is implicated in inflammation, autoimmunity, and cancer.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple citations to disease-associated mutations discussed in the Introduction and Results sections.

claim: The first high-resolution structure of a full-length PLC-γ isozyme has been determined.
source: Here, we describe the first high-resolution structure of a full-length PLC-γ isozyme and use it to underpin a detailed model of their membrane-dependent regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by the crystallographic data presented in the Results section and Supplementary file 1.

claim: An interlinked set of regulatory domains integrates basal autoinhibition, tyrosine kinase engagement, and scaffolding functions with phosphorylation-dependent allosteric control of phospholipase activation.
source: Notably, an interlinked set of regulatory domains integrates basal autoinhibition, tyrosine kinase engagement, and additional scaffolding functions with the phosphorylation-dependent, allosteric control of phospholipase activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis presented in Figure 1 and the mechanistic model described in the Results and Discussion sections.

claim: The structure explains why mutant forms of PLC-γ isozymes found in several cancers have a wide spectrum of activities.
source: The model also explains why mutant forms of the PLC-γ isozymes found in several cancers have a wide spectrum of activities, and highlights how these activities are tuned during disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mutational analysis presented in Figures 5 and 6, showing varying levels of constitutive activation for different cancer-associated mutations.

claim: The 13 phospholipase C (PLC) isozymes expressed in humans preferentially hydrolyze the membrane phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to generate the second messengers diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3).
source: The 13 phospholipase C (PLC) isozymes expressed in humans preferentially hydrolyze the membrane phospholipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) to generate the second messengers diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) (Harden and Sondek, 2006; Kadamur and Ross, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PLC enzymes, supported by the cited references.

claim: Diacylglycerol is retained within membranes where it recruits and activates numerous proteins including conventional isoforms of protein kinase C.
source: Diacylglycerol is retained within membranes where it recruits and activates numerous proteins including conventional isoforms of protein kinase C.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of diacylglycerol as a second messenger.

claim: IP3 diffuses throughout the cytosol where it binds to IP3 receptors embedded in endoplasmic reticulum leading to mobilization of sequestered calcium.
source: In contrast, IP3 diffuses throughout the cytosol where it binds to IP3 receptors embedded in endoplasmic reticulum leading to mobilization of sequestered calcium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of IP3 as a second messenger.

claim: PLC-mediated depletion of PIP2 modulates the activities of several ion channels and proteins with phosphoinositide-binding domains.
source: PLC-mediated depletion of PIP2 also modulates the activities of several ion channels and proteins with phosphoinositide-binding domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the regulatory role of PIP2 depletion.

claim: PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2 are unique among the PLCs in that they are directly activated by tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: The two PLC-γ isozymes, PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2, are unique among the PLCs in that they are directly activated by tyrosine phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a distinguishing feature of PLC-γ isozymes compared to other PLC families, supported by established knowledge.

claim: PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2 are phosphorylated on equivalent sites, Tyr783 and Tyr759, respectively, and this phosphorylation is typically required to stimulate phospholipase activity.
source: PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2 are phosphorylated on equivalent sites, Tyr783 and Tyr759, respectively, and this phosphorylation is typically required to stimulate phospholipase activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the key phosphorylation sites required for activation.

claim: Several classes of tyrosine kinases phosphorylate and activate the PLC-γ isozymes, including receptor tyrosine kinases and soluble tyrosine kinases.
source: Several classes of tyrosine kinases phosphorylate and activate the PLC-γ isozymes. These include a large number of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) including Trk receptors (Minichiello et al., 2002; Vetter et al., 1991) and many growth factor receptors such as epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) (Kim et al., 1991; Nishibe et al., 1990; Peters et al., 1992; Takahashi et al., 2001; Wahl et al., 1989). A second large group is soluble tyrosine kinases coupled to immune receptors and includes members of the Src, Syk, and Tec families (Law et al., 1996; Nakanishi et al., 1993; Schaeffer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple literature citations describing different kinase families that activate PLC-γ isozymes.

claim: The regulated, phosphorylation-dependent activation of PLC-γ1 and -γ2 controls numerous aspects of biology including proper development of the vascular, neuronal, and immune systems during embryonic development, adaptive immune responses, neuronal transmission, bone homeostasis, chemotaxis, and platelet aggregation.
source: The regulated, phosphorylation-dependent activation of PLC-γ1 and -γ2 controls numerous aspects of biology including proper development of the vascular, neuronal, and immune systems during embryonic development, adaptive immune responses, neuronal transmission, bone homeostasis, chemotaxis, and platelet aggregation (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference summarizing the biological roles of PLC-γ isozymes.

claim: PLC-γ1 is the most frequently (~40%) mutated gene in adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma.
source: In fact, PLC-γ1 is the most frequently (~40%) mutated gene in adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma, where mutant forms of the isozyme are presumed to drive oncogenesis through enhanced phospholipase activity coupled to elevated NFAT- and NF-κB-dependent transcription (Kataoka et al., 2015; Vaqué et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited genomic sequencing studies.

claim: Activating mutations in PLC-γ2 arise with high frequency (~30%) in patients with B cell leukemias treated with ibrutinib.
source: Moreover, activating mutations in PLC-γ2 arise with high frequency (~30%) in patients with B cell leukemias treated with ibrutinib (Woyach et al., 2014), a covalent inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical study.

claim: PLC-γ2 is a major BTK substrate and mutations in PLC-γ2 likely function as escape mutations, reactivating pathways controlling cell survival and proliferation that are usually rendered quiescent by ibrutinib treatment.
source: PLC-γ2 is a major BTK substrate and mutations in PLC-γ2 likely function as escape mutations, reactivating pathways controlling cell survival and proliferation that are usually rendered quiescent by ibrutinib treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between BTK and PLC-γ2 and the clinical observation of mutations arising during ibrutinib treatment.

claim: Mutated forms of the PLC-γ isozymes are found in patients with angiosarcomas.
source: Mutated, and presumably active, forms of the PLC-γ isozymes are also found in patients with angiosarcomas (Behjati et al., 2014), and several disorders associated with dysregulated immune responses (Ombrello et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012), inflammatory bowel disease (de Lange et al., 2017), and familial steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (Gbadegesin et al., 2015; Parker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical and genetic studies.

claim: A naturally occurring variant of PLC-γ2 that is moderately active is strongly associated with protection from late-onset Alzheimer's disease.
source: A naturally occurring variant of PLC-γ2 that is moderately active is strongly associated with protection from late-onset Alzheimer's disease (Magno et al., 2019; Sims et al., 2017) and highlights the notion that aberrant PLC activity can be either deleterious or beneficial depending on the context.
evidence: This is supported by the cited genetic association studies.

claim: For the vast majority of mutant forms of PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2, an increase in lipase activity has not been demonstrated directly.
source: However, for the vast majority of mutant forms of PLC-γ1 and PLC-γ2, an increase in lipase activity has not been demonstrated directly.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: The regulatory array of PLC-γ isozymes harbors the obligatory sites of tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: In particular, the regulatory array harbors the obligatory sites of tyrosine phosphorylation (Gresset et al., 2010; Kim et al., 1991; Nishibe et al., 1990), and also includes an SH2 domain (nSH2) required for tyrosine kinase binding (Bae et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies identifying phosphorylation sites and kinase binding domains.

claim: Removal or mutation of the cSH2 domain within the regulatory array results in robust and constitutive activation of PLC-γ isozymes in vitro and in cells.
source: The array also mediates basal autoinhibition of phospholipase activity, since removal or mutation of a second SH2 domain (cSH2) within the array results in robust and constitutive activation of PLC-γ isozymes in vitro and in cells (Gresset et al., 2010; Hajicek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: The regulatory array is completed by a split PH (sPH) domain and an SH3 domain, which modulate PLC activity by scaffolding numerous signaling and adaptor proteins.
source: The regulatory array is completed by a split PH (sPH) domain and an SH3 domain, which modulate PLC activity by scaffolding numerous signaling and adaptor proteins (Sherman et al., 2016; Walliser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies on protein-protein interactions.

claim: The other half of the autoinhibitory interface formed by the cSH2 domain has not been identified prior to this study.
source: For example, the other half of the autoinhibitory interface formed by the cSH2 domain has not been identified, and how this domain enforces autoinhibition of phospholipase activity is unknown.
evidence: This describes a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Phosphorylated Tyr783 in PLC-γ1 binds with nanomolar affinity to the cSH2 domain.
source: Phosphorylated Tyr783 in PLC-γ1 binds with nanomolar affinity to the cSH2 domain, and this engagement presumably couples a large, but ill-defined conformational rearrangement within the array to activation (Gresset et al., 2010; Hajicek et al., 2013; Poulin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited biochemical binding studies.

claim: An alternative model posits engagement of RTKs by the cSH2 domain as an initial step required for activation.
source: However, even these few mechanistic details are under debate since an alternative model posits engagement of RTKs by the cSH2 domain as an initial step required for activation (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes an alternative hypothesis from the literature.

claim: There are no structures of full-length PLC-γ isozymes prior to this study.
source: There are no structures of full-length PLC-γ isozymes.
evidence: This describes the state of structural knowledge before this study.

claim: The structure of PLC-γ1 was determined at 2.5 Å resolution.
source: The 2.5 Å crystal structure (Supplementary file 1) of essentially full-length rat PLC-γ1 readily explains the autoinhibition of the PLC-γ isozymes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental result supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The regulatory array sits atop the conserved catalytic core and blocks the core from productively engaging membranes.
source: In particular, the regulatory array sits 'atop' the conserved catalytic core and blocks the core from productively engaging membranes (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The overall structure of PLC-γ1 is highly electronegative.
source: In addition, the overall structure is highly electronegative (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and this property will also inhibit lipase activity by disfavoring interactions with negatively charged membranes.
evidence: This is based on electrostatic calculations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The overall negative charge of the PH domain indicates that it is unlikely to bind phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate as previously reported.
source: In particular, the overall negative charge of the PH domain indicates that it is unlikely to bind phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate as previously reported (Falasca et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrostatic properties observed in the structure, contradicting a previous report.

claim: For PLCs to hydrolyze membrane-embedded PIP2, the hydrophobic ridge of the catalytic TIM barrel must insert into lipid bilayers.
source: For PLCs to hydrolyze membrane-embedded PIP2, the hydrophobic ridge of the catalytic TIM barrel must insert into lipid bilayers (Ellis et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous structural studies of PLC enzymes.

claim: In PLC-γ1, the hydrophobic ridge interacts with portions of the sPH domain in the regulatory array, which is expected to block membrane engagement.
source: However, in the case of PLC-γ1, the hydrophobic ridge interacts with portions of the sPH domain in the regulatory array; this arrangement is expected to effectively block membrane engagement.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and represents a mechanism of autoinhibition.

claim: The active site of PLC-γ1 is fully solvent-exposed and could presumably hydrolyze soluble substrates not embedded in lipid bilayers.
source: As implied by the visibility of the Ca2+ cofactor, the active site is fully solvent-exposed and could presumably hydrolyze soluble substrates not embedded in lipid bilayers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation of the active site accessibility.

claim: Two major interfaces lock the regulatory array on top of the catalytic core: the sPH domain interacting with the hydrophobic ridge of the TIM barrel, and loops of the cSH2 domain interacting with the C2 domain.
source: Two major interfaces lock the regulatory array on top of the catalytic core. The first is the aforementioned sPH domain interacting with the hydrophobic ridge of the TIM barrel (Figure 1c). Here, residues from the sPH domain interdigitate with residues of the hydrophobic ridge in a 'zipper-like' arrangement. A second interface is formed between loops of the cSH2 domain and the C2 domain of the catalytic core (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figures 1c and 1d.

claim: The BG and EF loops of the cSH2 domain clasp prominent turns of the C2 domain.
source: In this case, the BG and EF loops of the cSH2 domain clasp prominent turns of the C2 domain—almost as if the loops are pinching the C2 domain.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The sPH and cSH2 domains within the regulatory array brace each other through the C-terminal portion of the SH3 domain that lies between them.
source: The two interfaces between the regulatory array and catalytic core do not overlap, but the sPH and cSH2 domains within the regulatory array brace each other through the C-terminal portion of the SH3 domain that lies between them (Figure 1e): picture an arch with the tail end of the SH3 domain acting as the keystone.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1e.

claim: When Tyr783 is phosphorylated, it will compete with the C2 domain for binding to the cSH2 domain.
source: Therefore, when Tyr783 is phosphorylated, we propose that it will compete with the C2 domain for binding to the cSH2 domain.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on the structural observation that the same loops of cSH2 interact with both the C2 domain and phosphorylated Tyr783.

claim: Competition between phosphorylated Tyr783 and the C2 domain for the cSH2 domain would disengage the cSH2 domain from the C2 domain to initiate a rearrangement of the regulatory array relative to the catalytic core.
source: This competition would presumably disengage the cSH2 domain from the C2 domain to initiate a rearrangement of the regulatory array relative to the catalytic core.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the structural observations.

claim: A wholesale rearrangement of the regulatory array relative to the catalytic core is required for productive membrane engagement by PLC-γ1.
source: Indeed, the structure suggests that a wholesale rearrangement of the regulatory array relative to the catalytic core is required for productive membrane engagement by PLC-γ1 (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement and the requirement for membrane access.

claim: Previous SAXS studies showed that phosphorylation of PLC-γ1 is coupled to a conformational change.
source: This idea is consistent with previous studies using small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) that showed phosphorylation of PLC-γ1 is coupled to a conformational change that has yet to be defined (Bunney et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited SAXS study.

claim: The overall structure of PLC-γ1 supports the multivalent scaffolding properties of the PLC-γ isozymes required for proper signaling.
source: The overall structure of PLC-γ1 also supports the multivalent scaffolding properties of the PLC-γ isozymes required for proper signaling (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010; Rouquette-Jazdanian et al., 2012; Timsah et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural accessibility of binding domains, supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Both the nSH2 and SH3 domains are organized within the overall structure for unfettered access to cognate ligands.
source: In particular, both the nSH2 and SH3 domains are organized within the overall structure for unfettered access to cognate ligands (Figure 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The phosphotyrosine-binding pocket of the nSH2 domain is fully solvent exposed and is the major site for engagement of phosphorylated RTKs.
source: For example, the phosphotyrosine-binding pocket of the nSH2 domain is fully solvent exposed and the major site for engagement of phosphorylated RTKs (Bae et al., 2009; DeBell et al., 1999; Poulin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by cited binding studies.

claim: The canonical polyproline-binding site of the SH3 domain is positioned to readily engage various proteins including SLP-76, Cbl, and Vav1.
source: Likewise, the canonical polyproline-binding site of the SH3 domain is positioned to readily engage various proteins. Relevant examples include the scaffolding protein SLP-76 (Deng et al., 2005), the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cbl (Tvorogov and Carpenter, 2002), and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Vav1 (Braiman et al., 2006; Knyazhitsky et al., 2012; Sherman et al., 2016)—all of which must be engaged by PLC-γ1 for the proper clustering of T cell receptors and subsequent downstream signaling.
evidence: This is a structural observation supported by cited functional studies.

claim: The monomeric GTPase Rac2 binds the sPH domain of PLC-γ2 to elevate lipase activity.
source: In addition, the monomeric GTPase Rac2 binds the sPH domain of PLC-γ2 to elevate lipase activity (Piechulek et al., 2005; Walliser et al., 2008) and the equivalent surface within the sPH domain of PLC-γ1 is fully exposed to solvent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies and structural observations.

claim: Binding of Rac2 would not disrupt the overall structure of autoinhibited PLC-γ2, but may stabilize an active conformation once PLC-γ2 is engaged with membranes.
source: This last observation suggests that binding of Rac2 would not disrupt the overall structure of autoinhibited PLC-γ2. Rather, Rac2 may stabilize an active conformation of PLC-γ2 once PLC-γ2 is engaged with membranes as previously suggested (Walliser et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural accessibility of the Rac2 binding site and cited functional studies.

claim: The canonical phosphotyrosine-binding site of the cSH2 domain is buried in the structure of PLC-γ1.
source: In counterpoint to the above examples, the canonical phosphotyrosine-binding site of the cSH2 domain is buried in the structure of PLC-γ1.
evidence: This is a direct structural observation.

claim: The buried phosphotyrosine-binding site of the cSH2 domain is presumably reserved as the 'trigger' for phospholipase activation upon engagement of pTyr783.
source: This site is presumably reserved as the 'trigger' for phospholipase activation upon engagement of pTyr783.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and known activation mechanism.

claim: pTyr783 functions as an intramolecular ligand that can effectively compete for the buried surface of the cSH2 domain.
source: Therefore, pTyr783 is suggested to function as an intramolecular ligand that can effectively compete for the buried surface of the cSH2 domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement and binding properties.

claim: Tyr783 in PLC-γ1 is presumed to be the primary site of phosphorylation coupled to enzyme activation.
source: Tyr783 in PLC-γ1 is presumed to be the primary site of phosphorylation coupled to enzyme activation (Gresset et al., 2010; Kim et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Eight additional tyrosines in PLC-γ1 are phosphorylated (positions 186, 472, 481, 771, 775, 959, 977, and 1254), but these sites appear dispensable for RTK-dependent activation in cells.
source: Eight additional tyrosines are phosphorylated (positions 186, 472, 481, 771, 775, 959, 977, and 1254), but these sites appear dispensable for RTK-dependent activation in cells (Bunney et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited functional study.

claim: Activation of PLC-γ1 by soluble tyrosine kinases requires phosphorylation of both Tyr775 and Tyr783.
source: In contrast, activation of PLC-γ1 by soluble tyrosine kinases requires phosphorylation of both Tyr775 and Tyr783 (Serrano et al., 2005) and this situation is similar for PLC-γ2 where the analogous tyrosines (positions 753, 759) are also phosphorylated during phospholipase activation (Humphries et al., 2004; Ozdener et al., 2002; Rodriguez et al., 2001; Watanabe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Wild-type PLC-γ1 and mutated forms that are constitutively active in cells have essentially identical capacity to hydrolyze the soluble substrate WH-15 in vitro.
source: This is in fact the case since wild-type PLC-γ1 and a set of mutated forms that are constitutively active in cells (Hajicek et al., 2013) (also see below) have essentially identical capacity to hydrolyze WH-15 in vitro (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 3a.

claim: When the membrane-embedded substrate XY-69 in lipid vesicles was presented to wild-type and mutant PLCs, there was a dramatic difference in hydrolytic rates, with wild-type PLC-γ1 having very low specific activity while mutated forms were up to 30-fold more active.
source: In contrast, XY-69 is a fluorescent substrate of PLCs that was specifically designed to embed into lipid bilayers (Huang et al., 2018). When XY-69 in lipid vesicles was presented to the same set of PLCs, there was now a dramatic difference in hydrolytic rates (Figure 3b). Wild-type PLC-γ1 had very low specific activity, while the mutated forms were up to 30-fold more active.
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Discrimination between wild-type and mutant PLC-γ1 was greatly diminished when XY-69 was solubilized in detergent micelles.
source: This discrimination presumably reflects the capacity of mutations to disrupt the interface between the regulatory domains and the catalytic core to favor a form of PLC-γ1 better able to engage PIP2 in membranes. Discrimination was greatly diminished—albeit not completely eliminated—when XY-69 was solubilized in detergent micelles (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Autoinhibition arises from the overall spatial arrangement of PLC-γ1 that prevents it from productively engaging membranes.
source: These results are consistent with the postulation that autoinhibition arises from the overall spatial arrangement of PLC-γ1 that prevents it from productively engaging membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined structural and functional data.

claim: Mutations that destabilize the autoinhibited arrangement concomitantly relieve autoinhibition and allow PLC-γ1 better access to membranes and PIP2.
source: Mutations that destabilize this arrangement are proposed to concomitantly relieve autoinhibition and allow PLC-γ1 better access to membranes and PIP2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data.

claim: All-atom accelerated molecular dynamics simulations of PLC-γ1 reproducibly highlighted a flexible set of regulatory domains relative to a virtually static catalytic core.
source: In particular, all-atom simulations of PLC-γ1 reproducibly highlighted a flexible set of regulatory domains relative to a virtually static catalytic core (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Flexibility of the regulatory domains increased for simulations of a constitutively active mutant form of PLC-γ1 harboring the D1165H substitution.
source: Moreover, this flexibility increased for simulations of a constitutively active mutant form of PLC-γ1 harboring a single substitution (D1165H) within the C2 domain at the interface with the phosphotyrosine-binding site of the cSH2 domain (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For both wild-type and mutant PLC-γ1, the correlated motions indicate that the regulatory domains tended to move as a relatively rigid block.
source: For both wild-type and mutant PLC-γ1, the correlated motions indicate that the regulatory domains tended to move as a relatively rigid block (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The D1165H substitution disrupts the proximal hydrogen-bonding network and results in the partial unfolding of the β5 and β6 strands of the C2 domain during simulations.
source: Substitution of Asp1165 to His (D1165H) disrupts the proximal hydrogen-bonding network and results in the partial unfolding of the β5 and β6 strands of the C2 domain during simulations.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations.

claim: The collapse of the β5/β6 region in the D1165H mutant is linked to an approximately 30° rotation of the cSH2 domain as it moves toward the C2 domain by approximately 10 Å.
source: The collapse of this region is linked to an approximately 30° rotation of the cSH2 domain as it moves toward the C2 domain by approximately 10 Å.
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations.

claim: Movements of the C2 and cSH2 domains are propagated to the rest of the regulatory array due to its propensity to move as a block.
source: The relative movements of the C2 and cSH2 domains are propagated to the rest of the regulatory array due to its propensity to move as a block.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlated motion analysis from simulations.

claim: Movements are essentially identical for a constitutively active mutant form of PLC-γ1 harboring two substitutions (Y747E+R748E) within the phosphotyrosine-binding site of the cSH2 domain.
source: Movements are essentially identical for a constitutively active mutant form of PLC-γ1 harboring two substitutions (Y747E+R748E) within the phosphotyrosine-binding site of the cSH2 domain and on the opposite side of the interface from Asp1165 (Figure 4—figure supplements 1, 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a result from computational simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplements.

claim: Diverse mutations within the cSH2/C2 domain interface will favor similar movements.
source: This result suggests that diverse mutations within the cSH2/C2 domain interface will favor similar movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of movements observed for different mutations in simulations.

claim: The PLC-γ isozymes are frequently mutated in several leukemias and lymphomas.
source: The PLC-γ isozymes are frequently mutated in several leukemias (Burger et al., 2016; Kataoka et al., 2015) and lymphomas (Choi et al., 2015; da Silva Almeida et al., 2015; Kiel et al., 2015; Vaqué et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited genomic studies.

claim: Sites of substitution in PLC-γ1 in adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma are found throughout the entire primary sequence with clusters at several hotspots.
source: In particular, PLC-γ1 is the most frequently mutated protein in adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma (Kataoka et al., 2015). In this disease, sites of substitution in PLC-γ1 are found throughout the entire primary sequence with clusters at several hotspots (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a based on genomic data from the cited study.

claim: When the entire set of substitutions is mapped onto the structure of autoinhibited PLC-γ1, the majority of sites localize to the interfaces formed between the PLC core and the regulatory array.
source: This rather uninformative arrangement is dramatically clarified when the entire set of substitutions is mapped onto the structure of autoinhibited PLC-γ1 (Figure 5b). Now, the majority of sites localize to the interfaces formed between the PLC core and the regulatory array.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b by mapping mutations onto the crystal structure.

claim: Most cancer-associated substitutions in PLC-γ1 disrupt the placement of the regulatory domains atop the core to disfavor autoinhibition.
source: This three-dimensional clustering strongly suggests that most cancer-associated substitutions in PLC-γ1 disrupt the placement of the regulatory domains atop the core to disfavor autoinhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural localization of mutations.

claim: In a panel of PLC-γ1 isozymes expressed in HEK293 cells, cancer-associated substitutions at the autoinhibitory interfaces produced a spectrum of constitutively active phospholipases, sometimes exceeding 1500-fold greater activity than wild-type PLC-γ1.
source: Indeed, in a panel of PLC-γ1 isozymes expressed in HEK293 cells, cancer-associated substitutions at these interfaces produced a spectrum of constitutively active phospholipases—sometimes exceeding 1500-fold greater activity than wild-type PLC-γ1 (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Cancer-associated mutations within the equivalent regions of PLC-γ2 produced similar enhancements, indicating conserved regulation between the two isozymes.
source: Cancer-associated mutations within the equivalent regions of PLC-γ2 produced similar enhancements, indicating conserved regulation between the two isozymes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cancer-derived mutations outside the autoinhibitory interfaces generally produced the smallest increases in basal lipase activities, but these increases were nonetheless significant in comparison to the wild-type isozyme.
source: Cancer-derived mutations outside the autoinhibitory interfaces generally produced the smallest increases in basal lipase activities—but these increases were nonetheless significant in comparison to the wild-type isozyme (Figure 5c, inset).
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 5c inset.

claim: Substitutions outside the autoinhibitory interfaces may increase the affinity of the active form of PLC-γ1 for membranes, as likely for R48W located in the PH domain near the presumed interface with membranes.
source: Based on the sites of mutation within the structure of autoinhibited PLC-γ1, three mechanisms are likely. First, substitutions may increase the affinity of the active form of PLC-γ1 for membranes. This option is likely the case for R48W located in the PH domain near the presumed interface with membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural location of the mutation.

claim: Substitutions might disrupt interactions provided by the keystone residues of the SH3 domain that buttress the organization of the sPH and cSH2 domains needed to maintain autoinhibition.
source: Second, substitutions might disrupt interactions provided by the keystone residues of the SH3 domain that buttress the organization of the sPH and cSH2 domains needed to maintain autoinhibition. Representative substitutions include R687W and R753H and additional examples are found in both PLC-γ1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and -γ2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of these residues.

claim: R687W in PLC-γ1 is analogous to R665W in PLC-γ2 and arises in patients with relapsed chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated with ibrutinib.
source: Of note, R687W is analogous to R665W in PLC-γ2 and arises in patients with relapsed chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated with ibrutinib (Woyach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical study.

claim: Mutations within the nSH2 domain, such as Q606R and D625Y, are near the binding site for phosphotyrosine and may increase affinity for phosphorylated kinases.
source: Finally, mutations within the nSH2 domain, for example Q606R and D625Y, are near the binding site for phosphotyrosine (Bae et al., 2009) and may increase affinity for phosphorylated kinases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural location of the mutations near the phosphotyrosine binding site.

claim: Cancer-associated mutations in PLC-γ1 have an untapped reserve of lipase activity that is at least partially released by EGF stimulation.
source: This result indicates an untapped reserve of lipase activity that is, at least partially, released by these cancer-associated mutations in response to EGF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing enhanced activity upon EGF stimulation.

claim: R48W, which occurs at the predicted interface of the active isozyme with membranes, shows abnormally elevated lipase activity only at high concentrations of EGF.
source: In contrast, R48W occurs at the predicted interface of the active isozyme with membranes and abnormally elevated lipase activity of PLC-γ1(R48W) manifests only at high concentrations of EGF.
evidence: This is a primary experimental result shown in Figure 6b.

claim: P867R and D1165H likely destabilize the inactive ensemble of PLC-γ1 while simultaneously favoring active forms of the isozyme.
source: This functional difference possibly reflects a mechanistic difference: P867R and D1165H likely destabilize the inactive ensemble of PLC-γ1 while simultaneously favoring active forms of the isozyme; in contrast, R48W has no substantive effect on the inactive population under these conditions and presumably only stabilizes the active isozyme once bound to membranes (Figure 6b, lower graph).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional differences observed in dose-response experiments.

claim: The lipase activity of mutant PLC-γ isozymes should be dependent on cellular context.
source: Regardless of the mechanistic details, these functional results suggest important biological ramifications. Namely, the lipase activity of mutant PLC-γ isozymes should be dependent on cellular context.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data showing context-dependent activation.

claim: PLC-γ1 or -γ2 harboring mutations such as R48W that preferentially stabilize active ensembles may be essentially quiescent until the isozymes are activated by phosphorylation.
source: For example, PLC-γ1 or -γ2 harboring mutations such as R48W that preferentially stabilize active ensembles may be essentially quiescent until the isozymes are activated by phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional behavior of R48W.

claim: More subtly activating substitutions may contribute to cancer in cells with high levels of active kinases such as upon the overexpression of EGFR or other growth factor receptors.
source: However, the more subtly activating substitutions may nonetheless contribute to cancer in cells with high levels of active kinases such as upon the overexpression of EGFR or other growth factor receptors—situations with widespread clinical relevance (Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data and cited clinical relevance.

claim: The structure of full-length, autoinhibited PLC-γ1 provides a first clear view of the regulated activation of the PLC-γ isozymes.
source: The structure of full-length, autoinhibited PLC-γ1 provides a first clear view of the regulated activation of the PLC-γ isozymes.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The catalytic core is conserved among all PLCs and is prevented from spuriously hydrolyzing PIP2 by a set of interdependent regulatory domains stationed to preclude access of the active site to membranes.
source: The overall picture is of a catalytic core that is conserved among all PLCs and that is prevented from spuriously hydrolyzing PIP2 by a set of interdependent regulatory domains stationed to preclude access of the active site to membranes.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: The regulatory domains are organized to integrate numerous molecular inputs that ultimately control phospholipase activity and mediate necessary scaffolding functions.
source: Additionally, the regulatory domains are organized to integrate numerous molecular inputs that ultimately control phospholipase activity and mediate necessary scaffolding functions (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the structural and functional findings illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The nSH2 domain is optimally positioned to readily bind phosphorylated kinases and align them to promote the phosphorylation of Tyr783 needed for activation of PLC-γ1.
source: Importantly, the nSH2 domain is optimally positioned to readily bind phosphorylated kinases and align them to promote the phosphorylation of Tyr783 needed for activation of PLC-γ1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement of the nSH2 domain.

claim: The equivalent surface of the cSH2 domain is buried through interactions with the C2 domain and is unlikely to initiate engagement of kinases.
source: Although capable of engaging phosphorylated portions of kinases (Groesch et al., 2006), the equivalent surface of the cSH2 domain is buried through interactions with the C2 domain and is unlikely to initiate engagement of kinases as previously suggested (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation that the cSH2 phosphotyrosine binding site is buried, contradicting a previous model.

claim: The two SH2 domains might work in concert upon receptor engagement to facilitate the binding of phosphorylated Tyr783 to the cSH2 domain.
source: However, the two SH2 domains might work in concert upon receptor engagement to facilitate the binding of phosphorylated Tyr783 to the cSH2 domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the full-length structure with a structure of the SH2 domains bound to FGFR1.

claim: Upon binding FGFR1, the βA/αA loop of the nSH2 domain is rearranged to accommodate pTyr766 of FGFR1 and this rearrangement leads to additional movements of the cSH2 domain.
source: Based on this comparison, the βA/αA loop of the nSH2 domain is rearranged to accommodate pTyr766 of FGFR1 and this rearrangement leads to additional movements of the cSH2 domain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the full-length structure, equivalent movements upon binding FGFR1 would open the surface of the cSH2 domain that binds pTyr783, effectively priming it to engage pTyr783.
source: In the full-length structure, equivalent movements upon binding FGFR1 would open the surface of the cSH2 domain that binds pTyr783, effectively priming it to engage pTyr783.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: Engagement of pTyr783 by the cSH2 domain is presumed to unlatch the cSH2 domain from the catalytic core and initiate a massive rearrangement of the regulatory domains with respect to the core before the core can engage membranes and hydrolyze PIP2.
source: Engagement of pTyr783 by the cSH2 domain is presumed to unlatch the cSH2 domain from the catalytic core and initiate what is likely to be a relatively massive rearrangement of the regulatory domains with respect to the core before the core can engage membranes and hydrolyze PIP2.
evidence: This is the proposed activation mechanism based on structural and functional data.

claim: Most of the substitutions and small deletions in PLC-γ isozymes that are linked to cancers or autoimmune disease occur at the interfaces between the core and regulatory domains.
source: In particular, most of the substitutions and small deletions in these isozymes that are linked to cancers (Burger et al., 2016; Kataoka et al., 2015; Woyach et al., 2014) or autoimmune disease (Ombrello et al., 2012) occur at the interfaces between the core and regulatory domains based on the structure of autoinhibited PLC-γ1.
evidence: This is based on mapping disease-associated mutations onto the crystal structure.

claim: Disease-associated mutations disrupt the interfaces between core and regulatory domains, release autoinhibition, and favor conformations that engage membranes to promote constitutive phospholipase activity.
source: These mutations disrupt these interfaces, release autoinhibition, and favor conformations that engage membranes to promote constitutive phospholipase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural localization of mutations and functional data.

claim: Shifted conformational equilibria may explain the supra-activation of mutant forms of PLC-γ1 by EGFR.
source: Shifted conformational equilibria may also explain the supra-activation of mutant forms of PLC-γ1 by EGFR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data showing enhanced activation by EGFR.

claim: Mutant forms of PLC-γ1 that are predisposed to be 'open' may have a greater propensity to bind EGFR and a lower probability of turning off.
source: That is, mutant forms of PLC-γ1 that are predisposed to be 'open' may also have a greater propensity to bind EGFR and a lower probability of turning off.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conformational properties of mutants.

claim: Constitutive activation of mutant PLC-γ isozymes varies greatly, ranging from approximately 10-fold to over 1500-fold.
source: Constitutive activation varies greatly, ranging from approximately 10-fold to over 1500-fold, with important cellular implications: highly active forms are expected to drive downstream signaling under all circumstances while more subtly active forms are likely to promote disease only within specific cellular contexts.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Mutated forms of PLC-γ2 (R665W or L845F) that arise in patients treated with ibrutinib have normal calcium homeostasis until B cell receptors are activated, at which point intracellular calcium levels rise and remain elevated.
source: B cells harboring either mutant of PLC-γ2 possess normal calcium homeostasis until B cell receptors are activated, at which point intracellular calcium levels rise and remain elevated, while in the equivalent wild-type case, calcium homeostasis is rapidly reestablished (Woyach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited functional study.

claim: Both R665W and L845F mutant forms of PLC-γ2 have essentially wild-type phospholipase activity at low levels of expression but are hypersensitive to activation by Rac2.
source: Both mutant forms have essentially wild-type phospholipase activity at low levels of expression but are hypersensitive to activation by Rac2 (Walliser et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited functional study.

claim: Once active, the R665W and L845F mutant forms of PLC-γ2 are stabilized at membranes by binding to Rac2 and are slow to return to their autoinhibited state.
source: These results suggest that once active, the mutant forms of PLC-γ2 are stabilized at membranes by binding to Rac2. That is, the mutations are cryptic until the isozymes are activated, at which point the mutated PLC-γ2 isozymes are slow to return to their autoinhibited state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited functional data.

claim: Similar context-dependent activation of mutant forms of the PLC-γ isozymes should occur upon activation by kinases.
source: Similar context-dependent activation of mutant forms of the PLC-γ isozymes should also occur upon activation by kinases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data for EGFR activation.

claim: PLC-γ1(R48W) has essentially wild-type phospholipase activity until co-expressed with high levels of active EGFR.
source: PLC-γ1(R48W) provides an example: it has essentially wild-type phospholipase activity until co-expressed with high levels of active EGFR.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Analogous scenarios of context-dependent activation may be widespread in cancers where tyrosine kinases are constitutively active upon substitution, truncation, fusion, or overexpression.
source: Analogous scenarios may be wide-spread in cancers where tyrosine kinases are constitutively active upon substitution, truncation, fusion, or overexpression—all conditions shown to activate PLC-γ1 (Arteaga et al., 1991; Peles et al., 1991).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data and cited examples of kinase activation in cancer.

claim: The activation of RTKs by stromal components contributes to treatment-resistant cancers and roles for wild-type and mutant PLC-γ isozymes under these conditions need to be explored.
source: Alternatively, the activation of RTKs by stromal components contributes to treatment-resistant cancers (Straussman et al., 2012) and roles for wild-type and mutant PLC-γ isozymes under these conditions need to be explored.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions based on cited work on treatment resistance.

claim: The interfacial regulation of the PLC-γ isozymes suggests promising avenues for their isozyme-specific, allosteric modulation by small molecules.
source: On a final note, the interfacial regulation of the PLC-γ isozymes suggests promising avenues for their isozyme-specific, allosteric modulation by small molecules to advance related chemical biology and on-going drug discovery.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the structural findings.

claim: Compounds that inhibit the movement of the regulatory domains relative to the catalytic core should prevent membrane engagement and consequent PIP2 hydrolysis.
source: Namely, compounds that inhibit the movement of the regulatory domains relative to the catalytic core should also prevent membrane engagement and consequent PIP2 hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential inhibitor mechanisms based on the structural model.

claim: Such compounds might treat cancers and immune diseases driven by constitutively active forms of the PLC-γ isozymes.
source: Such compounds might treat cancers and immune diseases driven by constitutively active forms of the PLC-γ isozymes.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Allosteric modulators that stabilize active forms of the PLC-γ isozymes might bolster immunotherapies or provide promising leads for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Conversely, allosteric modulators that stabilize active forms of the PLC-γ isozymes might bolster immunotherapies (Guittard et al., 2018) or provide promising leads for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease where a naturally occurring hypermorphic variant of PLC-γ2 is linked to protection from this disease (Magno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on cited work on immunotherapy and Alzheimer's disease.

claim: The crystallized construct of PLC-γ1 contains residues 21–765 and 791–1215, with an internal deletion (Δ25) replacing residues 766–790 with a flexible linker.
source: In addition, an internal loop of 25 residues connecting the cSH2 and SH3 domains was removed and replaced with a flexible linker; we refer to this internal deletion as Δ25 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, also see Materials and methods). The crystallized construct therefore contains residues 21–765 and 791–1215 of PLC-γ1.
evidence: This describes the construct design used for crystallization.

claim: The crystallized form of PLC-γ1 was autoinhibited in cells.
source: However, we have demonstrated previously that this loop is not directly required for autoinhibition (Gresset et al., 2010), and consistent with this notion, the crystallized form of PLC-γ1 was autoinhibited in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a functional validation of the crystallized construct shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The crystallized version of PLC-γ1 faithfully recapitulated the mutational activation of the wild-type enzyme.
source: While nuanced differences in regulation between the wild-type and crystallized version of PLC-γ1 cannot be excluded, the latter faithfully recapitulated the mutational activation of the wild-type enzyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a functional validation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deletion of the cSH2/SH3 domain loop had no measurable effect on the hydrodynamic radius or specific activity of the purified protein.
source: In addition, deletion of the cSH2/SH3 domain loop had no measurable effect on the hydrodynamic radius or specific activity of the purified protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), further demonstrating that removal of the loop did not significantly alter the biochemical properties of the enzyme.
evidence: This is a biochemical validation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
